title: How America Moved Giant Logs Before Trucks
fullText: In 1902, in a stand [music] of redwood on the northern California coast, a crew of 14 men spent 3 days felling a single tree. When it finally hit the ground, the impact registered on a seismograph 50 mi away. The trunk measured 17 ft across. It weighed an estimated 400 tons. And here is the question nobody asks. How did they move it? There were no trucks, no bulldozers, no paved roads anywhere near that forest. The nearest sawmill was 8 mi through dense timber and broken mountain terrain. And yet somehow that tree got out. Not just that one, millions of them. The biggest trees that have ever stood on the North American continent were hauled out of the deepest forests by men using horses, water, steam, and ideas so wild that most of them have been completely forgotten today. This is the story of how America moved giant logs before trucks existed. The forgotten machines, the dangerous men, [music] and the insane engineering that built a country out of timber. To understand any of [music] this, you have to first understand the trees. Because the forests that covered America before 1900 [music] were not the forests we have today. Not even close. When the first commercial [music] logging crews pushed into the Great Lakes region in the 1840s, they walked into a world of white pines [music] that had been growing for 400 years. Trees over 6 ft thick. Trees so tall [music] that 19th century photographs of them look fake. trees with trunks so [music] straight and clear that a single one could be cut into more than 10,000 board feet of lumber. And then came [music] the Pacific Northwest, Douglas fur, western red cedar, sitka spruce, trees that made the Great [music] Lakes pines look small. The largest specimens topped out at over 300 ft tall with trunks [music] 12 to 15 ft thick at the base. A single old growth Douglas fur could weigh more than 200 [music] tons. That is heavier than a fully loaded 18-wheeler. It is the weight of a small commercial airliner. And every single one of these trees once it was on the ground had to be moved. In the early days, the only answer was animals, specifically oxen and draft horses. A single team of oxen, six [clears throat] or eight pairs harnessed together, could drag logs that weighed [music] 20,000 lb or more. But the ground in a working forest is brutal. stumps, [music] mud, fallen branches, slopes, swamps. You cannot just drag [music] a giant log through that and expect to get anywhere. So loggers invented the skid road. [music] They felled smaller trees, stripped them, and laid them across the ground like railroad ties. Then they greased [music] these skids with bare fat, fish oil, or whatever else they had on hand. The big logs slid across the surface with shocking efficiency. A skilled bullhacker, the man who drove the ox team, could pull 30,000 lb [music] of timber over grease skids that would have stopped any wagon dead in its tracks. Those rough timber roads ran straight through company towns. The neighborhoods that grew up alongside them were full of cheap saloons, brothel, [music] and flophouses for the men who worked the timber. That is where we got the phrase skid row. It started in Seattle on a real skid road that ran down toward the harbor. A century later, the term means something else entirely. But it started here in the mud and grease of a logging operation. But oxen had a problem. They were slow. They tired. They could only work in cool weather on solid ground. And in a country racing to clear forests faster than anyone in human history had ever cleared forests, slow was not going to cut it. Enter Silus Overpack, a wagon [music] maker in Manaste, Michigan, who in 1875 looked at the problem of summer [music] logging and came up with one of the most distinctive machines in American history. The big wheels. Imagine two wooden wagon wheels, [music] each one nearly 10 ft tall, joined by a single axle. A log was chained underneath the axle, [music] so its front end was lifted off the ground. The back end dragged. Now suddenly, an ox team could pull logs across summer terrain that had been completely impossible before. No more waiting for winter snow to make the ground slick. No more being stuck for months out of the year. Overpack sold thousands of pairs of big wheels. They became so iconic that for a generation you could not look at a Michigan logging operation [music] without seeing them rolling through the woods. There are still a few preserved at [music] museums in the upper peninsula. They look like something out of a steampunk fever dream. They were the family sedan of the timber [music] industry for almost 40 years. But the real highway of the old logging world was not on land at all. It was the river. This was the genius of 19th century logging operations. You did not need to build roads. You did not need to lay rails. You just needed to get the log to a creek and gravity and snow melt would do the rest. Every spring when the rivers swelled with melting mountain snow, loggers would push millions of logs into the water and drive them downstream like cattle. The Ponobscot in Maine, the Clearwater in Idaho, the St. [music] Croy in Minnesota. Every major timber producing river in America became a flowing conveyor belt during [music] drive season. But this was not like floating a stick in a stream. We are talking about logs the size of telephone poles weighing tens of [music] thousands of pounds each. All moving together in a churning mass. When they jammed, they jammed catastrophically. A single log catching sideways [music] could pile up 30 ft high and stretch for half a mile up the river. These jams were so dangerous they had to be broken apart by hand by men called river pigs. The river pig was the cowboy of the eastern logging world. He wore cked boots which were leather work boots with steel spikes driven through the soles. He carried a long pike pole and his job was to run, jump and dance across moving logs in freezing white water, [music] prying jams loose, keeping the drive moving downstream. When a log jam was found, a key log had to be identified. The one log holding the whole pile in place. A river pig would climb onto the jam, find that log, and chop it free. Then he would run for his life. Because once that key log went, the entire jam came apart in seconds, and a wall of timber and water would sweep down the river. If you were still on it when it broke, [music] you were dead. There was no swimming through a log drive. The water was full of grinding, rolling timber moving at speeds nobody could outrun. River pigs had a saying, "Bury the dead and feed the living." Because every spring, several of them did not make it home. But the river drives had a limit. They needed water. And in the dry summer creeks of the Pacific Northwest and the Sierra Nevada, the water just was not there. So loggers invented the splash dam. A splash dam was a temporary timber dam built across a small creek. Crews would pile up logs behind it for weeks or months, letting a small stream slowly fill the reservoir. Then, on the day of the drive, they would knock out the supports. The dam blew. A wall of water exploded down the creek, carrying the entire stockpile [music] of logs miles downstream in minutes. It was effective. It was also an environmental catastrophe nobody fully understood at the time. Splash dams scoured creek beds down to bedrock. They wiped out [music] salmon runs that had supported indigenous communities for thousands of years. Some Pacific Northwest wersheds have never recovered even [music] a 100red years later. The Coke River in Oregon, the Scadget in Washington, dozens of others. Their salmon populations crashed during the splash dam era and never came back to the numbers they had before. It was a machine made out of wood [music] and gravity and it reshaped entire ecosystems. By the 1880s though, a new force was about to change. Logging forever steam. In 1881, a man named John Dolbeir was running a logging operation in [music] Hanold County, California. He was tired of losing oxen to exhaustion and [music] accidents. So, he sat down and designed something new. a small portable steam engine bolted to a wooden sled with a vertical winch drum. He called it [music] the steam donkey. The way it worked was simple. You set the donkey down at the landing. You ran a long steel cable out into [music] the woods, attached it to a log, and then you fired up the boiler. The cable would wind up onto the drum and that log, [music] no matter how big, came rolling and crashing through the underbrush at speeds no animal team could match. A single steamed donkey [music] operated by four or five men could do the work of 50 oxen. Suddenly crews shrank. Animal teams disappeared. The output of an operation tripled, then [music] quadrupled. Within 20 years, every major logging operation in [music] America had a steam donkey or a dozen. They had names painted on their boilers. The Black Maria, the Iron Mike, the Widow Maker. They sat in the forest hissing and pumping and yarding logs out of places no horse or ox [music] could ever go. If you are enjoying this deep dive into the forgotten machines of American industry, [music] take a second to hit that subscribe button. It is the only way to make sure stories like this keep showing up in [music] your feed. But getting logs to the landing was only half the problem. You still had to move them out of the mountains. And for that, the answer was steel. [music] Logging railroads were unlike anything else on rails. Standard locomotives could not handle the grades [music] or the tight curves of mountain logging operations. So engineers built specialty machines. The Shea locomotive designed in 1877 [music] by a Michigan logger named Ephraim Shea used vertical cylinders and a [music] flexible drive shaft to power every wheel on every truck. It could climb grades twice as steep as a regular train and grind around curves so tight [music] a normal locomotive would derail. The Climax and the Heisler followed similar designs. [music] These machines were ugly. They were slow. They sounded like the end of the world. And they could pull a chained string of loaded log cars up a thousand ft mountain on track that had been laid the week before. Logging companies [music] built tens of thousands of miles of temporary railroad in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The track moved [music] as the cutting moved. When a section of forest was logged out, crews would pull up the rails, load them onto flat cars, and lay them somewhere new. Some of these rail [music] beds are still visible today, deep in the second growth forests of Oregon, Washington, [music] and Northern California. hiking trails that follow oddly straight, level cuts through the woods. That is [music] what they are. Old logging grades abandoned a century ago. But even the Shea locomotive [music] had limits. You could not lay track up a vertical cliff. You could not run rails across a swamp. And so for the truly impossible terrain, loggers turned to the sky. The highle lead system was one of the most dangerous and ingenious machines ever invented. The idea was simple. Pick a tree at your landing site, the tallest one you can find. Climb it. Cut off the top. Rig it with steel cables and [music] pulleys. Now run a main cable all the way out to the cutting site. Anchor it to a smaller tree there. And you have a skyline. [music] Logs could be hooked to that cable, lifted entirely off the ground, and flown back to the landing through the air. It was incredible to watch. A 200 foot Douglas fur, a single log weighing 50 tons, sailing through the air over swamps and ravines [music] like it was nothing. But somebody had to climb that spar tree and rig it. And that somebody was the high climber. The high climber was a specialist. He was paid more than anyone else in the camp because his job was straight up suicidal. He would strap a pair of climbing spurs to his boots, loop a flexible steel rope around the tree trunk, and walk himself up 200 f feet of swaying timber, cutting off branches as he went. At [music] the top, he would chop the entire crown off the tree. A piece of wood that [music] might weigh several tons while standing on the trunk it had just been attached to. When that crown [music] fell, the whole tree would whip back and forth violently. The high climber had to ride that whip 200 ft in the air with no safety [music] equipment beyond his rope. They were the rock stars of the logging camps. They were also dying constantly. Falls, snapped cables, the whip itself [music] ripping a man loose. The phrase widow maker was originally about logging branches that fell from above without [music] warning, killing the man underneath, but it could just as easily have meant the spa tree job. In the dry mountain country of California and Nevada, crews tried something different. The flume, a logging flume, was a long V-shaped wooden trough, sometimes 50 mi long or more, that ran from a high mountain mill all the way down to a rail head in the valley. Water was diverted from a creek into the top of the flume, and logs and finished lumber would float down at 30 or 40 m an hour. Some men actually rode the flumes. There are old photographs from Tahoe and the Sierras showing flume riders sitting on planks hurtling down miles of wooden trough through the mountains. It was technically against company rules. It was also one of the most thrilling rides in 19th century America. The flumes were marvel. The Pacific Lumber Company in California operated one that ran for over 50 m. The Sanger Lumber Flume in the Sierras dropped 4,000 vertical feet from start to finish. They were wooden water slides for industrial timber, and they worked beautifully until the trees ran out. Through all of this, the logging industry had a quiet, ugly secret. The men were dying constantly. Modern OSHA statistics did not exist. Most companies did not even keep injury records. But what we can piece together from old hospital logs and county death records is brutal. In the Pacific Northwest around the turn of the century, somewhere around one in every 200 working loggers died on the job each year. That is not lifetime risk. That is annual. Crushed by [music] falling logs, drowned in river drives, decapitated by snapped steel cables that whipped through [music] the air faster than a bullet, killed by widowmaker branches falling from the canopy. There are old cemeteries in towns like Abedine, [music] Washington, and Eureka, California, where you can still walk among the [music] headstones of young men, 20, 25 years old, who never came home from a [music] single shift in the woods. The work paid well by the standards of the day. It also killed at rates that would shut down any modern [music] industry overnight. By the 1910s, change was finally coming. Two California companies, Halt and Best, had been experimenting with tracked [music] tractors. Steam-powered at first, then gasoline. These machines could crawl across mud, swamp, and soft ground [music] that no horse or ox could handle. Loggers were among the first customers. The Holt crawler became so iconic that the British military bought thousands of them during the First World War, used them as the basis for the first tanks, and helped [music] change warfare forever. After the war, Holton Best merged to form a new company. They called it Caterpillar. Yes, that Caterpillar, the yellow construction equipment [music] company that dominates the world today, started by hauling logs out of Pacific Northwest mud. And right alongside the crawlers, the first practical logging [music] trucks were starting to appear. Solid rubber tires, chain drives, engines just barely strong enough to pull a single log down a rough dirt road. By 1925, internal combustion was replacing steam in the woods. By 1940, the river drives were almost completely gone, replaced by trucks running on dirt and gravel [music] logging roads. The world that had moved logs with oxen, water, steam, and steel cable had ended. And it had ended fast. Less than 20 years from the first crawler to the near total dominance of the truck. But here is the part that does not get talked about. The thing that all of this was actually doing. Those forests, the ones with trees so big they would not fit in a modern logging truck, those forests were over a thousand years old. The oldest trees in the Pacific Northwest had been alive when the Vikings [music] reached Greenland. Some had been alive longer than that. In a span of about 70 years, between roughly 1870 and 1940, the American logging industry took down over 90% of those forests. [music] Today, less than 5% of original American old growth remains. The biggest [music] trees, the ones that astounded the early loggers and inspired all of those wild machines, they are almost entirely gone. The salmon runs that fed indigenous nations for 10,000 years collapsed during the Splash Dam era and never fully recovered. Whole ecosystems that took thousands of years to build were turned into railroad ties, mine timbers, and house frames in less than a single human lifetime. [music] The cities of America were quite literally built out of those forests. The houses on every block of older neighborhoods in San Francisco, Chicago, Boston are framed in old growth, Douglas fur, and white pine. You are still living inside [music] those trees. You just do not know it. The men who moved them, the bullwhackers and river pigs and high climbers and donkey punchers, they have mostly faded into folklore. Paul Bunan was [music] based on real men working in real woods doing things that would terrify any [music] modern industrial worker. The machines they used, the big wheels and steam donkeys and Sha locomotives and high lead systems sit rusting in forest [music] preserves and small town museums across the country. Most people walk past them and [music] have no idea what they are looking at. But for almost a century, they were the entire backbone of how America got built. Before the truck, before the bulldozer, [music] before the chainsaw, there was an army of men, animals, water, and steam hauling out the biggest [music] trees the continent ever grew. And every house, every railroad tie, every piece of timber in this country traces back to them. Next time you walk through a second growth forest in the Pacific Northwest, look around. The straight, level cuts running through the trees. Those are old logging grades. The rusty cables you sometimes find tangled [music] in the underbrush. Those are the remains of high lead operations. The strange level shelves cut into hillsides. Splash dam sites where a creek used to be a reservoir for a few weeks every spring. The forest is still full of ghosts. Ghosts of an industry. Ghosts of the men who worked it and ghosts of trees that will not grow [music] back in our lifetime or our children's lifetime or possibly ever again. If you made it this far, you are exactly the kind of person who keeps stories like this alive. [music] So, do me a favor.
